narrative:
The model predicted a 57.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly 6th decile among accepted students) signaled that your performance placed you near the bottom of your class. Your first-year ranking had a similar but smaller effect, also placing you in the lowest decile against an average around 6th decile for accepted applicants. These two academic standing measures together created the largest part of the negative outlook.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 34 it was below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated the score itself as a factor that slightly improved the odds of passing. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were less influential in the final decision.

To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your class standing or retaking the LSAT to demonstrate clearer evidence that you can pass the bar. Consider reapplying once you have new results that directly address these weaknesses. (248 words)
